steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the History section of an encyclopedia article on the Ada programming language: why the US Department of Defense wanted a new language, how Ada was designed and chosen, its early reception and compilers, the DoD mandate, and where it ended up being used.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why the DoD wanted a common language (1970s, HOLWG)
- The requirements documents (Strawman to Steelman)
- The design competition and the choice of Ada
- Early reception and the first compilers
- The Ada mandate in the US and other NATO countries
- Later use in safety-critical and commercial systems
- Ada 95

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Why a new language
  - 1970s: DoD worried about number of languages in embedded computer system projects; many obsolete or hardware-dependent, none supported safe modular programming
  - 1975: High Order Language Working Group (HOLWG) formed to reduce the number, find or create a language for DoD and UK Ministry of Defence requirements
  - many iterations starting from original straw-man proposal -> language eventually named Ada
  - high-level languages in use for such projects: over 450 in 1983 -> 37 by 1996
- Requirements
  - HOLWG crafted the Steelman language requirements, a series of documents
  - many existing languages formally reviewed; 1977 conclusion: none met the specs
  - requirements created by DoD in The Department of Defense Common High Order Language program, 1978
  - predecessors in order: "Strawman", "Woodenman", "Tinman", "Ironman"
  - focus: embedded computer applications; reliability, maintainability, efficiency
  - included exception handling, run-time checking, parallel computing
  - no existing language met them sufficiently -> contest to create one; winner became Ada; followed Steelman closely but not exactly
- Competition
  - requests for proposals; four contractors: Red (Intermetrics, Benjamin Brosgol), Green (Honeywell, Jean Ichbiah), Blue (SofTech, John Goodenough), Yellow (SRI International, Jay Spitzen)
  - April 1978: Red and Green passed to next phase after public scrutiny
  - May 1979: Green chosen, named Ada after Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (Ada Lovelace)
  - influenced by LIS, developed by Ichbiah's group in the 1970s
  - preliminary reference manual in ACM SIGPLAN Notices, June 1979
  - Military Standard reference manual approved December 10, 1980 (Lovelace's birthday), number MIL-STD-1815 (her birth year)
  - 1981: Tony Hoare's Turing Award speech criticized Ada as overly complex and hence unreliable; later seemed to recant in foreword to an Ada textbook
- Early days
  - lots of attention; backers predicted it might become dominant for general purpose programming, not just defense
  - Ichbiah: within ten years only two languages would remain, Ada and Lisp
  - early compilers struggled with the large, complex language; slow compile-time and run-time performance, primitive tools
  - vendors spent most effort passing the government-required Ada Compiler Validation Capability (ACVC) validation suite, another novel feature of the effort
  - first validated implementation: NYU Ada/Ed translator, certified April 11, 1983; implemented in SETL
  - commercial compilers/tools: Alsys, TeleSoft, DDC-I, Advanced Computer Techniques, Tartan Laboratories, Irvine Compiler, TLD Systems, Verdix
  - computer manufacturers in defense/aerospace: Concurrent Computer Corporation, Cray Research, Inc., Digital Equipment Corporation, Harris Computer Systems, Siemens Nixdorf Informationssysteme AG
- Mandate
  - 1991: DoD required Ada for all software (Ada mandate); exceptions often granted
  - effectively removed 1997 as DoD embraced commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) technology
  - other NATO countries: required for NATO command and control systems etc.; mandated/preferred for defense in Sweden, Germany, Canada
  - late 1980s / early 1990s: compilers faster, but barriers remained, e.g. tasking model unlike what real-time programmers were used to
- Later use
  - safety-critical features -> commercial projects where bugs are severe: avionics, air traffic control, Ariane 4 and 5 rockets, satellites/space, railway, banking
  - Boeing 777 Primary Flight Control System (fly-by-wire); fly-by-wire for Eurofighter Typhoon, Saab Gripen, Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor; DFCS replacement for Grumman F-14 Tomcat
  - Canadian Automated Air Traffic System: 1 million lines of Ada (SLOC); distributed processing, distributed Ada database, object-oriented design
  - UK iFACTS (Interim Future Area Control Tools Support) designed and implemented in SPARK Ada
  - French TVM in-cab signalling on TGV; metro suburban trains in Paris, London, Hong Kong, New York City
- Ada 95
  - went beyond Steelman; general-purpose as well as embedded systems; added object-oriented programming features

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the 1970s the US Department of Defense (DoD) was concerned about how many different programming languages were being used for its embedded computer system projects. Many of these languages were obsolete or hardware-dependent, and none of them supported safe modular programming. So in 1975 a working group was formed, the High Order Language Working Group (HOLWG), to reduce this number by finding or creating a programming language that would generally be suitable for the requirements of the department and also of the UK Ministry of Defence. There were many iterations, beginning with an original straw-man proposal and the language that came out at the end was named Ada. The total number of high-level programming languages in use for these projects went from over 450 in 1983 down to 37 by 1996.

HOLWG crafted the Steelman language requirements, which were a series of documents stating the requirements they felt a programming language should satisfy. Many existing languages were formally reviewed, but in 1977 the team concluded that no existing language met the specifications. The requirements were created by the United States Department of Defense in The Department of Defense Common High Order Language program in 1978. The documents before it were called, in order, "Strawman", "Woodenman", "Tinman" and "Ironman". The requirements were focused on the needs of embedded computer applications, and they emphasised reliability, maintainability, and efficiency. They also included exception handling facilities, run-time checking, and parallel computing.

Since no existing language met these criteria well enough, a contest was called to create a language that would be closer to meeting them. The design that won this contest became the Ada programming language. The language followed the Steelman requirements closely, but not exactly.

Requests for proposals for a new programming language were issued and four contractors were hired to develop their proposals. These were under the names Red (Intermetrics led by Benjamin Brosgol), Green (Honeywell, led by Jean Ichbiah), Blue (SofTech, led by John Goodenough) and Yellow (SRI International, led by Jay Spitzen). In April 1978, after public scrutiny, the Red and Green proposals went to the next phase. In May 1979 the Green proposal, which was designed by Jean Ichbiah at Honeywell, was chosen. It was given the name Ada, after Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace, who is usually known as Ada Lovelace. The proposal was influenced by the language LIS, which Ichbiah and his group had developed in the 1970s. The preliminary Ada reference manual was published in ACM SIGPLAN Notices in June 1979. The Military Standard reference manual was approved on December 10, 1980, which was Ada Lovelace's birthday, and it was given the number MIL-STD-1815 in honor of the year she was born. In 1981 Tony Hoare used his Turing Award speech to criticize Ada for being too complex and therefore unreliable, but later he seemed to recant this in the foreword he wrote for an Ada textbook.

  - lots of attention; backers predicted it might become dominant for general purpose programming, not only defense
  - Ichbiah: in ten years only Ada and Lisp would remain
  - early compilers struggled; slow compile-time and run-time performance, primitive tools
  - vendors' effort mostly on passing the government-required ACVC validation suite
  - first validated: NYU Ada/Ed translator, certified April 11, 1983, written in SETL
  - commercial vendors: Alsys, TeleSoft, DDC-I, Advanced Computer Techniques, Tartan Laboratories, Irvine Compiler, TLD Systems, Verdix
  - defense/aerospace manufacturers: Concurrent Computer Corporation, Cray Research, Inc., Digital Equipment Corporation, Harris Computer Systems, Siemens Nixdorf Informationssysteme AG
- mandate

  - NATO: required for command and control etc.; mandated/preferred in Sweden, Germany, Canada

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the 1970s the US Department of Defense (DoD) was concerned about how many different programming languages were being used for its embedded computer system projects. Many of these languages were obsolete or hardware-dependent, and none of them supported safe modular programming. So in 1975 a working group was formed, the High Order Language Working Group (HOLWG), to reduce this number by finding or creating a programming language that would generally be suitable for the requirements of the department and also of the UK Ministry of Defence. There were many iterations, beginning with an original straw-man proposal and the language that came out at the end was named Ada. The total number of high-level programming languages in use for these projects went from over 450 in 1983 down to 37 by 1996.

HOLWG crafted the Steelman language requirements, which were a series of documents stating the requirements they felt a programming language should satisfy. Many existing languages were formally reviewed, but in 1977 the team concluded that no existing language met the specifications. The requirements were created by the United States Department of Defense in The Department of Defense Common High Order Language program in 1978. The documents before it were called, in order, "Strawman", "Woodenman", "Tinman" and "Ironman". The requirements were focused on the needs of embedded computer applications, and they emphasised reliability, maintainability, and efficiency. They also included exception handling facilities, run-time checking, and parallel computing.

Since no existing language met these criteria well enough, a contest was called to create a language that would be closer to meeting them. The design that won this contest became the Ada programming language. The language followed the Steelman requirements closely, but not exactly.

Requests for proposals for a new programming language were issued and four contractors were hired to develop their proposals. These were under the names Red (Intermetrics led by Benjamin Brosgol), Green (Honeywell, led by Jean Ichbiah), Blue (SofTech, led by John Goodenough) and Yellow (SRI International, led by Jay Spitzen). In April 1978, after public scrutiny, the Red and Green proposals went to the next phase. In May 1979 the Green proposal, which was designed by Jean Ichbiah at Honeywell, was chosen. It was given the name Ada, after Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace, who is usually known as Ada Lovelace. The proposal was influenced by the language LIS, which Ichbiah and his group had developed in the 1970s. The preliminary Ada reference manual was published in ACM SIGPLAN Notices in June 1979. The Military Standard reference manual was approved on December 10, 1980, which was Ada Lovelace's birthday, and it was given the number MIL-STD-1815 in honor of the year she was born. In 1981 Tony Hoare used his Turing Award speech to criticize Ada for being too complex and therefore unreliable, but later he seemed to recant this in the foreword he wrote for an Ada textbook.

In its early days Ada got a lot of attention from the programming community as a whole. Its backers and others predicted that it might become a dominant language for general purpose programming and not only for defense work. Ichbiah publicly said that within ten years there would only be two programming languages left, Ada and Lisp. The early Ada compilers struggled to implement such a large and complex language, and both compile-time and run-time performance tended to be slow and the tools were primitive. Compiler vendors put most of their effort into passing the massive, language-conformance-testing, government-required Ada Compiler Validation Capability (ACVC) validation suite, which was required in another novel feature of the Ada language effort.

The first validated Ada implementation was the NYU Ada/Ed translator, which was certified on April 11, 1983. NYU Ada/Ed is implemented in the high-level set language SETL. Several commercial companies started offering Ada compilers and development tools, including Alsys, TeleSoft, DDC-I, Advanced Computer Techniques, Tartan Laboratories, Irvine Compiler, TLD Systems, and Verdix. Computer manufacturers that had a significant business in defense, aerospace, or related industries also offered Ada compilers and tools on their platforms, and these included Concurrent Computer Corporation, Cray Research, Inc., Digital Equipment Corporation, Harris Computer Systems, and Siemens Nixdorf Informationssysteme AG.

In 1991 the US Department of Defense started to require the use of Ada for all software (the Ada mandate), although exceptions to this rule were often granted. The mandate was effectively removed in 1997, when the DoD began to embrace commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) technology. There were similar requirements in other NATO countries. Ada was required for NATO systems involving command and control and other functions, and it was the mandated or preferred language for defense-related applications in countries such as Sweden, Germany, and Canada.

By the late 1980s and early 1990s the performance of Ada compilers had improved, but there were still barriers to fully using Ada's abilities, including a tasking model that was different from what most real-time programmers were used to.

Because Ada has safety-critical support features, it is now used not only for military applications but also in commercial projects where a software bug can have severe consequences, for example avionics and air traffic control, commercial rockets such as the Ariane 4 and 5, satellites and other space systems, railway transport and banking.

For example the Primary Flight Control System, which is the fly-by-wire system software in the Boeing 777, was written in Ada. So were the fly-by-wire systems for the aerodynamically unstable Eurofighter Typhoon, Saab Gripen, Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor and the DFCS replacement flight control system for the Grumman F-14 Tomcat. The Canadian Automated Air Traffic System was written in 1 million lines of Ada (SLOC count). It had advanced distributed processing, a distributed Ada database, and object-oriented design. Ada is used in other air traffic systems too, for example the UK's next-generation Interim Future Area Control Tools Support (iFACTS) air traffic control system is designed and implemented using SPARK Ada.

It is also used in the French TVM in-cab signalling system on the TGV high-speed rail system, and in the metro suburban trains in Paris, London, Hong Kong and New York City.

The Ada 95 revision of the language went beyond the Steelman requirements. It targeted general-purpose systems as well as embedded ones, and it added features supporting object-oriented programming.

In the 1970s the US Department of Defense (DoD) became concerned by the number of different programming languages being used for its embedded computer system projects, many of which were obsolete or hardware-dependent, and none of which supported safe modular programming. The design that won this contest became the Ada programming language. The resulting language followed the Steelman requirements closely, though not exactly.

Requests for proposals for a new programming language were issued and four contractors were hired to develop their proposals under the names of Red (Intermetrics led by Benjamin Brosgol), Green (Honeywell, led by Jean Ichbiah), Blue (SofTech, led by John Goodenough)[4] and Yellow (SRI International, led by Jay Spitzen). In April 1978, after public scrutiny, the Red and Green proposals passed to the next phase. In May 1979, the Green proposal, designed by Jean Ichbiah at Honeywell, was chosen and named Ada, after Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace, usually known as Ada Lovelace. This proposal was influenced by LIS, a language that Ichbiah and his group had developed in the 1970s. The preliminary Ada reference manual was published in ACM SIGPLAN Notices in June 1979. The Military Standard reference manual was approved on December 10, 1980 (Ada Lovelace's birthday), and given the number MIL-STD-1815 in honor of her birth year. In 1981, Tony Hoare used his Turing Award speech to criticize Ada for being overly complex and therefore unreliable,[5] but subsequently seemed to recant in the foreword he wrote for an Ada textbook.[6]

During its early days Ada attracted much attention from the programming community as a whole. Its backers and others predicted that it might become a dominant language for general purpose programming and not only defense-related work.[7] Ichbiah publicly stated that within ten years, only two programming languages would remain: Ada and Lisp.[8] Early Ada compilers struggled to implement the large, complex language; both compile-time and run-time performance tended to be slow and tools were primitive.[7] Compiler vendors spent most of their efforts on passing the massive, language-conformance-testing, government-required Ada Compiler Validation Capability (ACVC) validation suite that was required in another novel feature of the Ada language effort.[8]

The first validated Ada implementation was the NYU Ada/Ed translator,[9] certified on April 11, 1983. NYU Ada/Ed is implemented in the high-level set language SETL.[10] Several commercial companies began offering Ada compilers and associated development tools, including Alsys, TeleSoft, DDC-I, Advanced Computer Techniques, Tartan Laboratories, Irvine Compiler, TLD Systems, and Verdix.[11] Computer manufacturers with a significant business in the defense, aerospace, or related industries also offered Ada compilers and tools on their platforms; these included Concurrent Computer Corporation, Cray Research, Inc., Digital Equipment Corporation, Harris Computer Systems, and Siemens Nixdorf Informationssysteme AG.[11]

In 1991, the US Department of Defense began to require the use of Ada (the Ada mandate) for all software,[12] though exceptions to this rule were often granted.[7] The Department of Defense Ada mandate was effectively removed in 1997, as the DoD began to embrace commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) technology.[7] Similar requirements existed in other NATO countries: Ada was required for NATO systems involving command and control and other functions, and was the mandated or preferred language for defense-related applications in countries such as Sweden, Germany, and Canada.[13]

By the late 1980s and early 1990s, Ada compilers had improved in performance, but there were still barriers to fully exploiting Ada's abilities, including a tasking model that differed from what most real-time programmers were used to.[8]

Because of its safety-critical support features, Ada is now used not only for military applications, but also in commercial projects where a software bug can have severe consequences, e.g., avionics and air traffic control, commercial rockets such as the Ariane 4 and 5, satellites and other space systems, railway transport and banking.[14]

For example, the Primary Flight Control System, the fly-by-wire system software in the Boeing 777, was written in Ada, as were the fly-by-wire systems for the aerodynamically unstable Eurofighter Typhoon,[15] Saab Gripen,[16] Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor and the DFCS replacement flight control system for the Grumman F-14 Tomcat. The Canadian Automated Air Traffic System was written in 1 million lines of Ada (SLOC count), and featured advanced distributed processing, a distributed Ada database, and object-oriented design. Ada is also used in other air traffic systems; for example, the UK's next-generation Interim Future Area Control Tools Support (iFACTS) air traffic control system is designed and implemented using SPARK Ada.[17]

It is also used in the French TVM in-cab signalling system on the TGV high-speed rail system, and the metro suburban trains in Paris, London, Hong Kong and New York City.[14,18]

The Ada 95 revision of the language went beyond the Steelman requirements, targeting general-purpose systems as well as embedded ones, and adding features that support object-oriented programming.[19]
